Glucose is an aldohexose, so it shows most of the reactions of an aldehyde — but not all of
them, and the exception is the point of this question.
(a) **Hydroxylamine** reacts: NH₂OH condenses with the –CHO to give glucose oxime ✓
(b) **Acetic anhydride** reacts: all five hydroxyl groups are acetylated to give glucose
pentaacetate ✓
(d) **Br₂/H₂O** reacts: this mild oxidant converts the aldehyde to a carboxyl, giving gluconic
acid ✓
(c) **Sodium bisulphite** does **not** react ✗
NaHSO₃ forms an addition product with simple aldehydes and methyl ketones, but glucose
exists overwhelmingly in the cyclic hemiacetal form, with only a trace in the open-chain
aldehyde form at any moment. The ring, plus the bulk of the surrounding hydroxyls, prevents
the bisulphite addition.
This failure was one of the observations that showed glucose is cyclic rather than a simple
open-chain aldehyde — as was its failure to give the Schiff's test.
∴ sodium bisulphite.

For a weak base the hydroxide concentration comes from Ostwald's dilution law:
[OH⁻] = √(Kb × C)
Substitute Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² and C = 0.01 M = 10⁻² M:
[OH⁻] = √(1.0 × 10⁻¹² × 10⁻²)
= √(10⁻¹⁴)
= 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹
The square root is the step to get right: adding the exponents gives −14, and halving that
gives −7, not −14 or −12.
So [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹ ✓
It is worth noticing that this is the same as the hydroxide concentration in pure water, so
this base is so weak that at this dilution it barely affects the pH at all — a strictly exact
treatment would have to include the water's own ionisation.
∴ 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|1|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The Gabriel phthalimide synthesis makes **primary aliphatic amines only**, and both halves of
that restriction rule out three of the options.
The route is: phthalimide + KOH gives the potassium salt; that anion displaces halide from an
alkyl halide by **SN2**; alkaline hydrolysis then releases the amine.
**Primary only** — the nitrogen ends up with exactly one alkyl group, because the phthalimide
ring blocks any further substitution. So (b) the secondary amine and (c) the tertiary amine
cannot be made this way.
**Aliphatic only** — the key step is SN2 on an alkyl halide. An **aryl** halide will not undergo
SN2, since the ring carbon cannot be attacked from behind and the C–X bond has partial
double-bond character. So (d) aniline is impossible.
That leaves CH₃CH₂NH₂, a primary aliphatic amine, made from bromoethane ✓
This is precisely why the method is preferred over alkylating ammonia, which gives a mixture
of primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
∴ CH₃CH₂NH₂.

Nitrobenzene can be reduced to several different products, and which one you get depends
entirely on the reagent and the medium. That is what this question tests.
**Acidic medium** — Fe/HCl or Sn/HCl reduces it all the way to **aniline**, C₆H₅NH₂.
**Neutral medium** — Zn dust with NH₄Cl stops at the intermediate stage, giving
**phenylhydroxylamine**, C₆H₅NHOH.
**Strongly alkaline medium** — Zn dust with NaOH couples two molecules to give hydrazobenzene;
LiAlH₄ gives **azobenzene**, C₆H₅N=NC₆H₅.
Now check the options:
(a) Zn/NH₄Cl ⇒ aniline — wrong product; that reagent gives phenylhydroxylamine.
(b) LiAlH₄ ⇒ phenylhydroxylamine — wrong; LiAlH₄ gives azobenzene.
(c) Fe/HCl ⇒ nitrosobenzene — wrong; Fe/HCl gives aniline.
(d) Zn dust and NH₄Cl ⇒ phenylhydroxylamine ✓ correctly matched.
∴ option (d).
